I am a 46-year-old farmer with six years of experience, so I know what works on my land in Quzhou County. The wheat–maize double cropping is my main system and feeds my family of four, so I devote 55 mu to it. The other 11 mu I split between stevia and sweet potato because they bring in better cash than grain alone. I have a well, which means I am not completely at the mercy of the weather, but I still watch my costs carefully.

For the wheat already in the ground, this spring I will irrigate three times—at green-up, jointing, and grain filling—and split my nitrogen application to avoid waste. I use an improved high-yielding wheat variety because the seeds are reliable and the yield is much better than traditional ones. For the summer maize that follows the wheat harvest, I will switch to no-tillage direct seeding. Time is tight between wheat harvest and maize sowing in June, and I have learned that hybrid maize seed performs best with minimal soil disturbance as long as I irrigate at the critical growth stages. 

My 5 mu of stevia is a cash crop for the sweetener market. It needs steady moisture, so I will irrigate four times and give it extra potassium to improve leaf quality. I plant improved stevia seedlings. My 6 mu of sweet potato is partly for household consumption and partly for sale. Sweet potato needs deep ploughing and ridging to form tubers properly, and it is hungry for potassium, so I will plough the field and apply heavy K fertilizer, irrigating three times.

I keep pesticide use moderate—two applications for most crops—because over-spraying cuts into profits and I have not had severe pest outbreaks in recent years.
